taskTitle: Twelve HTTP status codes, by the book

checks.detail: a 7-step plan, read from the schema reply
2 phases had the tools designed for them

penalties.label: Cited pages that were never opened
penalties.detail: 1 of 3 cited URLs were never opened: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110

finalText:
I've checked all 12 codes against RFC 9110, "HTTP Semantics" (June 2022). Every reason phrase, section number and quote below comes from https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html.

**Is RFC 9110 still current?** I couldn't fully confirm this. The info page https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110 returned HTTP 404, so I couldn't check its "Obsoleted by" list or its errata. Searches turned up nothing that replaces RFC 9110. Its own header says it obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615 and 7694, and parts of 7230.

**Heuristic cacheability.** Section 15.1 of https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html says codes "defined as heuristically cacheable (e.g., 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 308, 404, 405, 410, 414, and 501 in this specification)" can be reused with heuristic expiration. It adds that "all other status codes are not heuristically cacheable." So from your list:
- **Cacheable:** 203, 206, 308, 405, 410, 414 and 501. Each of their own sections also says "A NNN response is heuristically cacheable."
- **Not cacheable:** 303, 307, 413, 421 and 422. None of their sections says otherwise, so the list and the section texts agree.
- **421:** Appendix B.3 notes that 421 "is no longer defined as heuristically cacheable since the response is specific to the connection (not the target resource)."

**Name changes.** One assumption in the plan was only half right:
- **413** really was renamed. RFC 7231 called it "413 Payload Too Large" (Section 6.5.11, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7231.html). RFC 9110 calls it "Content Too Large", and "Payload Too Large" no longer appears anywhere in it.
- **422** was not renamed from RFC 7231, because RFC 7231 never defined it (the page contains no "422"). RFC 9110 Appendix B.3 says 422 was "previously defined in Section 11.2 of [WEBDAV]" and moved into RFC 9110. It's now named "Unprocessable Content". I believe WebDAV called it "Unprocessable Entity", but I didn't open that document to check.
- **421** came from RFC 7540, and **308** from RFC 7538.

**About the quotes.** The page text wraps lines at fixed points, so the quotes join the wrapped lines with single spaces. I picked sentences with no hyphenated line breaks and no bracketed reference links.
